summary: This unit teaches you to use the instruments found in plant rooms and factories to measure pressure, temperature, flow, level, speed and electrical values. You will learn to plan a round of readings, work safely around pressure, heat and moving machinery, choose the right instrument and range, read scales and displays accurately, change between units, and understand a 4–20 mA signal. You will also learn to check instruments against a reference, look after them, and record and report readings properly.

blocks.p: Pumps, compressors, boilers, chillers and process lines are watched through their instruments. Operators and maintenance staff take readings on a regular **round**, write them on a **log sheet** and compare them with the normal range, so that a problem is spotted before it becomes a breakdown or an accident. This unit is for Level 2 trainees, who take and record readings, use portable instruments and check instruments against references, under supervision. You do not adjust plant controls.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Know which points to read, their normal ranges and units; get permission and tell the operator.
Work safely in a plant room
Control the hazards of pressure, hot surfaces, steam, moving machinery, electricity, noise and wet floors.
Pick the instrument and range for the quantity, the expected value, the accuracy needed and the conditions.
Read dial gauges and manometers; understand gauge, absolute and vacuum pressure; fit and remove a test gauge safely.
Use probe, dial, thermocouple, RTD and infrared thermometers, and know the limits of each.
Read flow meters, sight glasses and level displays; measure shaft speed with a tachometer.
Use electrical measurements in a plant
Measure current, resistance and insulation safely; understand a 4–20 mA signal and work out what it shows.
Avoid parallax and zero errors, work out scale divisions, and change between kPa, bar, psi, °C, °F and K.
Do a comparison check against a reference, judge pass or fail, and handle, store and label instruments correctly.
Write each reading at once with units, time and initials; report any reading outside its normal range.

blocks.h: Where you will meet these instruments in Jamaica

ul: Water pumping stations and treatment plants: pressure, flow, level and motor current.
Hotels and hospitals: boilers, hot-water systems, chillers, standby generators and water tanks.
Factories: bottling, food, dairy, sugar, rum, cement and bauxite or alumina plants.
Garages and workshops: air compressors and their receivers.

blocks.note: Many instruments in Jamaica are imported from the United States and are marked in **psi** and **°F**, while drawings, log sheets and newer instruments use **kPa, bar and °C**. Always write the unit with the number, and convert carefully (see the units section).
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order, and work through every example with a calculator. Then try the practice test and read every explanation. Normal ranges, tolerances and calibration intervals vary from plant to plant: this kit gives typical values, but on the job you follow the log sheet, the maker's manual and your supervisor.

sections.title: Planning a round and working safely

flow: Collect the log sheet and read the list of points and the normal range of each
Find any missing normal values in the maker's manual or the plant's operating procedure
Tell the supervisor and the plant operator what you will be doing and where
Put on the PPE the area needs
Check your own instruments: undamaged, calibration in date, zero or lead check done
Plan a safe route that keeps you clear of moving parts and hot lines

blocks.p: **Why know the normal range first?** If you know what a reading should be, you can spot at once a reading that is wrong or unsafe, and check it before you write it down. A reading taken without knowing what it should be is easy to misread and easy to ignore.

blocks.h: Plant room hazards and their controls

head: Hazard
Controls
rows: **Hot surfaces and steam**: pipes, boilers, tanks, flues
Gloves suited to heat, long sleeves, never touch a line before checking it; keep clear of steam vents and drains.
**Pressure**: lines, receivers and gauges that can leak or burst
Safety glasses; never loosen a fitting or remove a gauge under pressure; stand to one side of gauges, not in front of their faces; open valves slowly.
Guards stay on; tie back hair; no loose clothing, lanyards or jewellery; never reach past or through a guard.
Do not open panels; use meters and leads with a suitable CAT rating; resistance and insulation tests only on isolated circuits.
Hearing protection where signs say so, and near running compressors, generators and boilers.
**Slips and trips**: wet or oily floors, hoses, cables
Safety boots; report and clean up spills; keep walkways clear.
Read the labels and safety data sheets; gloves and goggles as required; wash hands.
Tell someone where you are and when you expect to finish.

blocks.h: Fitting and removing a test gauge

blocks.p: A test gauge is fitted to a **test point**: a small connection with its own **isolating valve** (gauge cock). You need the permission of the supervisor or the person in charge of the plant before you open or close any valve.

flow: Get permission and tell the operator
Check the test gauge: range suits the line, calibration in date, no damage, thread matches
Make sure the isolating valve is closed, then open the vent slowly to release any trapped pressure
Screw the gauge on with a spanner on the gauge's square or hex, never by twisting the case; hold the fitting with a second spanner; seal the thread as needed
Stand to one side and open the isolating valve slowly, so the pointer does not slam
Check for leaks; let the pointer settle; read square on; record
To remove: close the isolating valve, vent the pressure, check the gauge reads zero, then unscrew it

blocks.note: **Never unscrew a gauge or loosen a fitting while it is under pressure.** Air, water or steam can blow the gauge off, spray hot fluid or whip a hose. Close, vent, check zero, then remove.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Reflective tape** for an optical tachometer is stuck on the shaft **only while the machine is stopped and isolated**, by the person authorised to do it.
With the machine running, aim the light beam at the tape through the opening in the guard, from the distance the maker gives. The guard stays on.
A **contact tachometer** has a rubber tip pressed against the centre of the shaft end. It is used only where the shaft end can be reached safely; at Level 2, use the optical type.

blocks.note: Never tap a gauge hard to make the pointer move, never adjust a gauge or plant control you are not authorised to touch, and never stand in front of a gauge face when pressure is being applied.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Unit
Equal to
Notes
rows: Very small: used for air ducts and fans
The usual unit on metric gauges and log sheets
Close to the pressure of the atmosphere; common on compressors
Common on imported gauges; 1 bar ≈ 14.5 psi

head: Kind
Measured from
Example
rows: The pressure of the atmosphere. A gauge open to the air reads 0.
Almost all plant gauges. Sometimes written kPa(g) or psig.
A perfect vacuum. Absolute = gauge + atmospheric.
A line at 200 kPa gauge is at about 301 kPa absolute. Barometers read absolute pressure.
Below atmospheric. Shown as a minus reading on a compound gauge.
A pump suction at −20 kPa is 20 kPa below atmospheric: about 81 kPa absolute.
Across a filter or an orifice plate: a rising difference across a filter means it is getting blocked.

blocks.note: In the °F to °C formula, take away 32 **first**, then divide. Dividing first is the most common mistake. Check your answer with a known pair: water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F and boils at 100 °C = 212 °F (at sea level).
blocks.label: Tip

head: Quantity
Units
Useful facts
rows: Litres per minute (L/min), litres per second (L/s), cubic metres per hour (m³/h)
Metres (m), or per cent of the tank
A tank 3 m deep that is 75% full holds water 2.25 m deep
Measured with a vibration meter on bearing housings

sections.title: Choosing an instrument and reading it accurately

flow: Decide what you must measure and in which units
Find the expected value and choose a range that covers it with room to spare
Check the accuracy and resolution are good enough for the job
Think about the conditions: heat, water, dust, vibration, moving or live parts
Choose contact or non-contact; check the CAT rating for electrical work
Check it is undamaged, working and in date for calibration; read the maker's instructions

head: To measure
Instruments
rows: Dial (Bourdon tube) gauge, digital gauge, U-tube manometer (low pressures), barometer (the atmosphere), compound gauge (vacuum and pressure), pressure transmitter
Liquid-in-glass and bimetallic dial thermometers, thermocouple, RTD, digital probe thermometer, infrared (non-contact) thermometer
Rotameter, orifice plate with differential pressure, magnetic flow meter, turbine meter, clamp-on ultrasonic meter, water meter
Sight glass, float, dipstick, pressure at the bottom of the tank, ultrasonic or radar sensor
Multimeter, clamp meter, insulation resistance tester
Hygrometer (humidity), vibration meter, sound level meter

ul: The normal reading should sit near the **middle** of the scale. A common rule is to choose a gauge whose full scale is about **twice the normal working pressure**, and never to let the working pressure go above about three-quarters of the scale.
A gauge whose range is **too small** can be over-pressured, which bends its tube, ruins its accuracy and can burst it.
A gauge whose range is **far too big** shows the reading in a tiny part of the scale, so it cannot be read accurately.
On a manual-range meter, start on the **highest** range when the value is unknown, then step down.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: How close a reading is to the true value
A gauge that reads 498 kPa when the true pressure is 500 kPa is accurate to 2 kPa at that point.
How close repeated readings of the same thing are to each other
A gauge that always reads 30 kPa low is repeatable but not accurate.
The smallest step a display or scale shows
A display showing 36.4 °C has a resolution of 0.1 °C.
The largest error allowed, as a percentage of full scale
A class 1 gauge of 0–1,000 kPa may be up to ±10 kPa out anywhere on its scale.

blocks.p: **Value of one small division = (difference between two numbered marks) ÷ (number of small divisions between them).** For example, numbered marks 2 bar apart with 10 small divisions between them: each small division is 2 ÷ 10 = 0.2 bar. A pointer three divisions past 6 reads 6 + 3 × 0.2 = **6.6 bar**.

ul: Look at the pointer **square on**, with your eye level with it, so that it covers its reflection if the dial has a mirror. Looking from the side gives a **parallax error**.
Wait for the pointer or display to **settle**. A probe thermometer needs time to reach the temperature of what it is in.
If a pointer shakes, read the middle of its swing and report it: a damper (snubber) may be needed.
Do a **zero check** before use: with nothing connected or the line vented, the gauge or meter should read zero. One that does not has a **zero error** and is not used until it has been checked.
Read digital displays carefully: check the decimal point, the unit and any minus sign.

blocks.p: Most dial pressure gauges use a **Bourdon tube**: a flattened metal tube bent into a C-shape, closed at one end. When pressure enters the tube it tries to **straighten**, and the closed end moves a little. Levers and gears magnify this movement and turn the pointer. Over-pressure bends the tube for good, so the gauge reads wrongly afterwards.

head: Instrument
How it works
Used for
rows: A curved tube straightens under pressure and moves a pointer
Most water, air, oil and steam lines
A thin flexible disc or capsule moves with pressure
Low pressures, and dirty or corrosive fluids
A clear tube of water or another liquid; pressure pushes the liquid down one side and up the other, and the difference in height shows the pressure
Very low pressures, such as in air ducts and gas lines; 1 mm of water is about 9.8 Pa
A Bourdon gauge whose scale reads below and above zero
Pump suctions and lines that can go under vacuum
Measures the pressure of the atmosphere (absolute)
A sensor gives an electrical signal; shown on a display or sent as 4–20 mA

head: Fitting
What it does
rows: Lets the gauge be isolated, vented and removed without shutting down the line.
A small restriction that steadies a pointer that shakes on a pump outlet or a compressor.
A looped pipe that fills with condensed water, so that hot steam cannot reach and damage the gauge.
Glycerine or oil inside the case damps vibration and pulsation and protects the movement.
Keeps corrosive, thick or dirty fluid away from the gauge's tube.

ul: A compressor's **pressure switch** stops the compressor when the receiver reaches its cut-out pressure and starts it again at the cut-in pressure.

The receiver's **safety valve** (relief valve) opens by itself and lets air out if the pressure rises too high, for example if the pressure switch fails. It is set at or below the receiver's maximum working pressure.
**Never** tie, wedge, block or adjust a safety valve. If one keeps lifting, report it: the pressure switch or the valve itself needs checking by an authorised person.
Never point compressed air at anyone, or use it to blow dust off clothes or skin: it can force air or dirt into the body.

head: What you see
Likely cause
What to do
rows: Pointer not on zero when vented
Zero error, often after over-pressure or a knock
Tag out of use; have it checked or replaced
Pulsation from a pump or compressor
Read the middle; report so a snubber or liquid-filled gauge can be fitted
Blocked connection, damaged movement, isolating valve partly closed
Report; do not tap it hard
Cracked glass, bent pointer, fogged face
Tag as faulty and report for replacement
Reading far from the normal range
A real plant problem, or a faulty gauge
Check with a second instrument if you can; record; report at once

head: Instrument
How it works
Good points
Limits
rows: A liquid in a thin glass tube expands as it warms and rises up a scale
Breaks easily; slow; read square on
A coiled strip of two different metals bends as it warms and turns a pointer
Tough; easy to read on pipes and tanks
Two different metals joined at the tip make a small voltage that rises with temperature; the instrument turns it into a temperature
Tough, cheap, wide range, up to very high temperatures (ovens, furnaces, exhausts, flues)
Less accurate than an RTD; needs the right type of extension cable (for example type K or J)
The resistance of a fine metal element, usually platinum, rises steadily with temperature
Accurate and stable: process pipes, tanks, hot water, cold rooms
Smaller range than a thermocouple; more delicate
A small part whose resistance changes greatly with temperature
Measures the infrared heat given off by a surface, without touching it
Fast; safe for hot, moving, live or hard-to-reach parts
Surface only; wrong on shiny surfaces; affected by steam, dust and distance

blocks.p: The most common RTD is the **Pt100**: a platinum element of **100 Ω at 0 °C**. Its resistance rises by about **0.385 Ω for each degree Celsius**, so it is about **138.5 Ω at 100 °C**. A rough temperature can be worked out from a resistance reading: temperature ≈ (resistance − 100) ÷ 0.385.

**Example.** A Pt100 reads 115.4 Ω. (115.4 − 100) ÷ 0.385 = 15.4 ÷ 0.385 = **40 °C**. The instrument's display does this for you; the calculation is useful for checking a sensor that is giving odd readings.

ul: **Emissivity**: dull, dark and painted surfaces give off heat well and read correctly. **Shiny, polished metal** (aluminium, stainless steel, galvanised steel) reflects heat from its surroundings and usually reads far too **low**. Aim at a painted or dull part, or stick on a patch of matt tape or paint and wait for it to reach the surface temperature.

**Spot size**: the thermometer reads the average of a circle that gets bigger with distance. A **12:1** instrument reads a spot about 50 mm across at 600 mm. Get close enough that the spot is smaller than the part.
It reads the **surface**, not the inside. It cannot read through glass, and steam, smoke or dust in the way give errors.
Its laser pointer only shows where it is aiming: do not shine it in anyone's eyes.

blocks.p: A **thermowell** is a closed metal pocket fitted into a pipe or tank, into which a sensor or thermometer is pushed. It protects the sensor from pressure, flow and corrosion, and lets the sensor be **taken out for checking or replacement without draining the line or letting out hot fluid**. Because the heat must pass through the wall of the well, the reading changes more slowly.

ul: After putting a probe into a liquid or a well, **wait** until the reading stops changing: the probe must reach the same temperature as what it is measuring.
Push the probe in to the depth the maker gives, and stir a liquid gently so that the probe sees its true temperature.
Hot water for a test should be hot, but not boiling; handle the container with gloves on a stable bench.

blocks.note: Water boils at 100 °C only at sea level. In the hills it boils at a lower temperature: about 98 °C in Mandeville, and lower still in the Blue Mountains. So 'boiling water' is not a reliable 100 °C check point in many parts of Jamaica. A mixture of crushed ice and water is a reliable 0 °C anywhere.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Flow, level, speed and electrical measurements

head: Meter
How it works
Notes
rows: A float rises in a tapered glass or plastic tube; the higher it rises, the greater the flow
Must be mounted upright; read the scale at the point on the float that the maker marks
A flat plate with a hole in it, fitted in the pipe; the flow is worked out from the pressure drop across it
Read with a differential pressure gauge or transmitter
Measures the small voltage made when a liquid that conducts electricity flows through a magnetic field
Only for liquids that conduct, such as water; not for oils or fuels
A small rotor spins in the flow; its speed shows the flow rate
Sends sound through the pipe wall
No need to cut the pipe
Counts the volume that has passed, in cubic metres
Read twice and subtract to find the volume used

head: Method
Notes
rows: A glass or clear tube on the side of the tank that shows the liquid level directly. It has isolating valves so that it can be shut off if the glass breaks.
A float rides on the surface and moves a pointer, or switches a pump on and off.
Simple; used to check other instruments.
Each metre of water adds about **9.8 kPa** (roughly 10 kPa). A gauge at the bottom reading 30 kPa means about 3 m of water above it.
Mounted on top of the tank; measures the time for a pulse to bounce off the surface.

ul: An **optical tachometer** counts the flashes of light reflected from a strip of tape on the shaft, and shows revolutions per minute (rpm).

Motors on Jamaica's **50 Hz** supply run a little below these speeds: a 2-pole motor at about 2,900 rpm (no-load speed close to 3,000), and a 4-pole motor at about 1,450 rpm (close to 1,500). Compare the reading with the nameplate.
A speed well below the nameplate figure can mean overload, a supply problem or a slipping belt; report it.

A **vibration meter** (vibration pen) is held on a bearing housing and reads the vibration, often in mm/s. The **trend** matters most: a reading that keeps rising week after week warns of a bearing or alignment problem before it fails.
A **hygrometer** measures humidity, for example in a store room or control room.
A **sound level meter** measures noise in decibels, to decide where hearing protection is needed.
Use a meter and leads with a **CAT rating** suitable for where you measure. Do not open panels: at Level 2, measurements in panels are made by authorised people.
An **ammeter** is connected in series; a **clamp meter** goes round one conductor only and needs no break in the circuit.

**Resistance**, for example of a heater element, is measured only with the circuit isolated, locked off and proved dead, with one end of the element disconnected so that other parts do not change the reading. A very high reading (OL) shows a broken element.
The insulation of a **motor winding** is checked with an **insulation resistance tester**, with the motor isolated and disconnected, at the test voltage given. A good winding reads high, in megohms.

blocks.p: Many **transmitters** (pressure, level, flow and temperature) turn their measurement into a small current that is sent along a pair of wires to a display or controller. **4 mA** means the **bottom** of the range (0%) and **20 mA** means the **top** of the range (100%). The span is 20 − 4 = **16 mA**.

ul: **Value = (current − 4) ÷ 16 × range**, plus the bottom of the range if it does not start at zero.
A current is used because it is not changed by the length or resistance of the wires, and it resists electrical noise.

Starting at 4 mA, not 0 mA, is called a **live zero**. A real reading of 0% still gives 4 mA, so **0 mA means a fault**: a broken wire, a lost supply or a failed transmitter. Readings well below 4 mA or above 20 mA also point to a fault.

blocks.p: **Working backwards:** current = 4 + (value ÷ range × 16). For 150 kPa on a 0–600 kPa transmitter: 150 ÷ 600 = 0.25; 0.25 × 16 = 4; 4 + 4 = **8 mA**.

Instruments drift over time, and they are damaged by knocks, drops, heat, vibration, over-pressure and over-range. A wrong reading can let a plant run at an unsafe pressure or temperature, spoil a product or hide a fault. **Calibration** means comparing an instrument with a **reference** that is known to be more accurate, recording the errors at several points across its range, and adjusting, correcting or replacing it if the errors are too big.

ul: Instruments are calibrated at the **interval in the plant's schedule** (often every 6 or 12 months), and after any damage, drop or doubtful reading.
The reference instruments are themselves calibrated by an accredited laboratory, so that every measurement can be traced back to a national standard.
A **calibration label** shows the instrument's number, the date of the check and the date the next one is due.
An instrument that is **out of date**, damaged or dropped is **tagged out of use** and sent for checking. It is never used 'just this once'.

blocks.h: Comparison check of a pressure gauge

flow: Fit the workshop gauge and an in-date reference gauge to the same test manifold, so both see the same pressure
Check fittings are tight; wear safety glasses; keep the supply below the lowest rating on the rig
Raise the pressure in steps across the scale, for example 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100%
At each step let both pointers settle and record both readings
Lower the pressure in the same steps and record again
Work out each error: workshop reading minus reference reading
Compare every error with the tolerance: pass and label, or fail and tag
Vent the pressure and check both gauges read zero before loosening any fitting

blocks.p: **Why falling readings too?** Friction and springiness in the movement can make a gauge read differently on the way up and on the way down. This difference is called **hysteresis**. A gauge must be within tolerance in both directions.

**Example.** The table is for a 0–600 kPa gauge with a tolerance of ±1.6% of full scale: 0.016 × 600 = **±9.6 kPa**. The largest error is +9 kPa (300 kPa, falling), which is inside ±9.6 kPa, so the gauge **passes**, but only just: note this so it is watched. An error is **positive** when the workshop gauge reads high and **negative** when it reads low.

ul: **Ice point (0 °C):** fill an insulated cup with **crushed ice**, add just enough clean water to fill the gaps, and stir. Push the stem in to the right depth without touching the bottom, wait until the reading is steady, and read it. The error is the reading minus 0 °C.
**Comparison:** put the workshop thermometer beside an in-date reference thermometer in warm water, at the same depth, stir, wait for both to settle and compare.
Too much water and too little ice makes the mixture warmer than 0 °C. Lumps of ice leave pockets of warmer water.
Carry and store instruments in their **cases**; never drop or throw them, or leave them where they can be knocked or stood on.
Keep them away from heat, direct sun, water and dust. Do not leave them in a hot vehicle.
Wipe them clean and dry after use.
Never use a gauge above its range, and open valves slowly so that the pointer does not slam against its stop.
Switch digital instruments off after use; take the batteries out if they will not be used for a long time.
Coil leads loosely; do not wrap them tightly round the instrument.
Sign instruments out and back in, so that each one can be traced.
Tag and report any instrument that is damaged, dropped or giving odd readings.

blocks.p: A log sheet is only useful if every entry is **complete, honest and readable**. Write each reading **straight away**, at the gauge, not from memory at the end of the round.

head: Point
Normal range
Reading
Time
Initials
Remarks
rows: Below range: reported to Mr Gordon 07:22

ul: Every reading has its **unit**, the **date and time**, and your **initials**.
Write the instrument used where the sheet asks, especially for portable instruments.
Write remarks about anything unusual: a leak, a strange noise, a smell, a damaged gauge, a guard missing.
Never change a reading to make it look normal, and never fill in a reading you did not take.

blocks.h: A reading outside its normal range

flow: Read it again carefully, square on, after it has settled
Check the instrument: zero, damage, the right scale and unit
Check with a second instrument if you can
Record the reading as it is, with a remark
Tell the supervisor or operator at once
Do not adjust plant controls yourself

blocks.p: **Trends** matter as well as single readings. A pressure, temperature or vibration reading that is still inside its range but has crept up every day is a warning. Compare today's readings with earlier ones and mention any steady change to your supervisor.

blocks.note: At the end of the round, check the log sheet is complete and signed, hand it in, return the instruments to their cases and report any instrument that needs attention.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can plan a round: log sheet, normal ranges, permission, PPE and instrument checks.
I can name the hazards in a plant room and the controls for each.
I can fit and remove a test gauge in the safe order: close, vent, check zero, remove.
I can change between kPa, bar and psi, and between °C, °F and K.
I can explain gauge, absolute, vacuum and differential pressure.
I can choose an instrument and a range for a measurement.
I can explain accuracy, repeatability, resolution and accuracy class.
I can work out the value of a scale division and read a scale without parallax error.
I can explain how a Bourdon tube gauge and a U-tube manometer work, and what snubbers and siphons are for.
I can compare thermocouples, RTDs and infrared thermometers, and use an infrared thermometer correctly.
I can explain what a thermowell does.
I can name flow and level instruments and say how they work.
I can measure shaft speed safely with an optical tachometer.
I can work out a value from a 4–20 mA signal and explain why 0 mA means a fault.
I can carry out a comparison check, work out the errors and decide pass or fail.
I can check a thermometer at the ice point.
I can handle, store and label instruments correctly.
I can record readings properly and report a reading outside its range.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: About 10 kPa per metre of water

terms: Absolute pressure
Pressure measured from a perfect vacuum: gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure.
Accuracy
How close a reading is to the true value.
Bourdon tube
The curved tube in a dial pressure gauge that straightens under pressure and moves the pointer.
Calibration
Comparing an instrument with a more accurate reference, recording its errors and correcting it.
Error
The instrument's reading minus the true (reference) value.
Gauge pressure
Pressure measured from atmospheric pressure; a gauge open to the air reads zero.
Hysteresis
A difference between readings taken with the value rising and with it falling.
Infrared thermometer
A thermometer that reads a surface's temperature from the heat it gives off, without touching it.
Live zero
The 4 mA bottom of a 4–20 mA signal, which lets a fault (0 mA) be told apart from a zero reading.
Log sheet
The form on which readings are recorded with their units, times and initials.
Manometer
A tube of liquid that shows a low pressure as a difference in liquid heights.
Parallax error
A reading error caused by looking at a pointer from one side.
Repeatability
How close repeated readings of the same thing are to each other.
Resolution
The smallest step a scale or display can show.
RTD
Resistance temperature detector: a sensor whose resistance rises steadily with temperature, such as a Pt100.
Safety valve
A valve that opens by itself to release pressure if it rises too high.
Siphon
A looped pipe that keeps hot steam away from a pressure gauge.
Snubber
A damper that steadies a gauge pointer on a pulsing line.
Tachometer
An instrument that measures shaft speed in revolutions per minute.
Thermocouple
A temperature sensor made of two different metals that gives a small voltage at the joined tip.
Thermowell
A closed pocket in a pipe or tank that holds a temperature sensor.
Transmitter
A device that turns a measurement into a signal, such as 4–20 mA, for a display or controller.
Vacuum
A pressure below the pressure of the atmosphere.
Zero error
A reading other than zero when nothing is being measured.

c1.title: The morning round at a May Pen pumping station
c1.text: Trainee Jodian is doing the morning round at a water pumping station near May Pen, Clarendon, with operator Mr Errol Gordon. The log sheet gives the normal discharge pressure of pump 2 as 350–450 kPa. The discharge gauge is marked 0–10 bar, with numbered marks every 1 bar and small divisions of 0.2 bar. The suction gauge is a compound gauge that reads from −100 kPa to +300 kPa. Jodian also checks the pump motor's bearing housings with an infrared thermometer; part of each housing is painted and part is bare, polished aluminium.

c2.title: The boiler room of an Ocho Rios hotel laundry
c2.text: Trainee Kemoy is learning the boiler room checks at a hotel laundry in Ocho Rios, St Ann, with maintenance supervisor Mrs Lorna Walker. The steam header has an imported gauge marked in psi, but the log sheet asks for kPa. The hot-water storage tank has a Pt100 sensor in one thermowell and an imported dial thermometer, marked in °F, in a second thermowell.

c3.title: The air compressor at a Black River garage
c3.text: At a garage in Black River, St Elizabeth, trainee Damion and mechanic Mr Vivian Clarke are checking the workshop air compressor. The receiver's plate gives a maximum working pressure of 12 bar, and the pressure switch stops the compressor at 10 bar. The receiver gauge reads 0–16 bar. With the receiver drained and its drain valve still open, the gauge reads 0.4 bar. The motor's nameplate says 1,450 rpm at 50 Hz, and the instructor has fitted reflective tape to the motor pulley while the compressor was stopped and isolated.

c4.title: Checking instruments at a Christiana dairy
c4.text: In the instrument room of a dairy in Christiana, Manchester, trainee Tamara and technician Mr Rohan Edwards check a 0–1,000 kPa workshop gauge against an in-date reference gauge on a test manifold. The tolerance is ±16 kPa. Readings (workshop / reference) rising: 0/0, 255/250, 510/500, 770/750, 1,015/1,000. Falling: 1,015/1,000, 772/750, 515/500, 262/250, 5/0. Next they check a dial thermometer in crushed ice and water.

c5.title: A tank level transmitter at a Runaway Bay hotel
c5.text: A hotel in Runaway Bay, St Ann, has a water storage tank 4 m tall. A level transmitter sends a 4–20 mA signal, set for 0–4 m, to a display in the maintenance office. The tank also has a sight glass, and a pressure gauge on the outlet at the bottom. Mr Dalton Shaw is showing trainee Nicola how the system works.

questions.q: The discharge pointer is three small divisions past the 4 bar mark. What is the pressure, and how does it compare with the log sheet?
o: 460 kPa, above the normal range
430 kPa, inside the normal range
46 kPa, far below the normal range
4.6 kPa, so the pump has stopped
questions.why: Each small division is 0.2 bar, so the reading is 4 + 3 × 0.2 = 4.6 bar. 1 bar = 100 kPa, so 4.6 bar = 460 kPa, which is above 450 kPa. Jodian should re-read it, record it with a remark and tell Mr Gordon at once.

questions.q: The suction gauge reads −20 kPa. What does this mean?
o: The gauge has a zero error of about 20 kPa
The pump is pushing water back down the suction
The suction is 20 kPa below atmospheric
The pipe holds 20 kPa less water than normal
questions.why: A minus reading on a compound gauge is a vacuum: a pressure below that of the atmosphere. −20 kPa gauge is about 101 − 20 = 81 kPa absolute. Pumps often draw their suction below atmospheric pressure when the water level is below the pump.

questions.q: On one housing the infrared thermometer reads 31 °C on the bare aluminium and 58 °C on the paint beside it. What should Jodian do?
o: Trust the 31 °C, since bare metal gives the truest reading
Hold the thermometer against the bare metal and try again
Record the reading taken on the paint, or on matt tape
Average the two readings and record about 45 °C
questions.why: Shiny metal reflects heat from its surroundings and gives off little of its own, so an infrared thermometer reads it far too low. A painted surface, or a patch of matt tape that has warmed up, gives a true reading. Write on the log where the reading was taken.

questions.q: The steam header gauge reads 100 psi. What should Kemoy write on the log sheet?
o: About 690 kPa
About 145 kPa
About 6.9 kPa
About 1,450 kPa
questions.why: 1 psi is about 6.9 kPa, so 100 psi × 6.9 ≈ 690 kPa (6.9 bar). Dividing instead of multiplying gives 14.5, a common mistake. Write the unit with the number.

questions.q: The Pt100 in the hot-water tank reads 123 Ω. About what is the water temperature?
o: About 23 °C
About 123 °C
About 100 °C
About 60 °C
questions.why: A Pt100 is 100 Ω at 0 °C and rises by about 0.385 Ω per °C: (123 − 100) ÷ 0.385 ≈ 60 °C. 123 °C would mean the water was far above boiling, and 23 Ω is the rise in resistance, not the temperature.

questions.q: The imported dial thermometer on the same tank reads 140 °F. Does it agree with the Pt100?
o: No: 140 °F is about 78 °C
Yes: 140 °F is 60 °C
No: 140 °F is about 108 °C
No: 140 °F is about 45 °C
questions.why: °C = (°F − 32) ÷ 1.8 = (140 − 32) ÷ 1.8 = 108 ÷ 1.8 = 60 °C, so the two instruments agree. Take away 32 first, then divide; dividing first gives the wrong answer of about 78 °C.

questions.q: Mrs Walker wants the dial thermometer checked against a reference. How does its thermowell help?
o: It lets the thermometer read faster than a bare probe
It turns the °F reading into °C for the log sheet
It lets it come out without draining the tank
It keeps the thermometer at exactly 0 °C for checking
questions.why: The thermowell is a closed pocket, so the thermometer can be drawn out for checking or replacement while the tank stays full and sealed. The price is a slower response, because heat must pass through the well's wall.

questions.q: With the receiver drained and its drain valve open, the gauge reads 0.4 bar. What does this tell Damion?
o: It has a zero error, so it must be checked or replaced
That is normal: every gauge reads a little above zero
The receiver is still under pressure and must not be touched
The gauge is fine; just tap the glass until it reads zero
questions.why: With the drain open the receiver is at atmospheric pressure, so the gauge should read zero. A gauge with a zero error, often from over-pressure or a knock, cannot be trusted across its scale. Tag it out of use and have it checked or replaced; never tap it hard.

questions.q: Another worker says the receiver's safety valve keeps hissing and offers to wire it shut. What should Mr Clarke say?
o: Yes, because the pressure switch already stops the compressor
No: it is the last protection against the receiver bursting
Yes, as long as someone watches the gauge while it runs
No, because a wired valve would make the gauge read high
questions.why: The safety valve releases pressure if the pressure switch fails, so it is the last protection against the receiver bursting. Never tie, block or adjust it. A valve that keeps lifting is a warning: report it so the switch and valve can be checked by an authorised person.

questions.q: Damion's optical tachometer reads 1,470 rpm on the motor pulley. What does this show?
o: The motor is running well below its rated speed
The tachometer is faulty: it should read 50
The motor is over-speeding and must be stopped
The motor is running at about its normal speed
questions.why: A 4-pole motor on a 50 Hz supply runs a little below 1,500 rpm: about 1,450 rpm at full load and a little faster at lighter load. 1,470 rpm is normal. The 50 on the nameplate is the supply frequency in hertz, not a speed.

questions.q: What is the largest error Tamara finds on the workshop gauge?
o: +15 kPa at 1,000 kPa
+20 kPa at 750 kPa, rising
+22 kPa at 750 kPa, falling
+12 kPa at 250 kPa, falling
questions.why: Error = workshop − reference. Rising: 0, +5, +10, +20, +15. Falling: +15, +22, +15, +12, +5. The largest is 772 − 750 = +22 kPa at 750 kPa on the way down.

questions.q: With a tolerance of ±16 kPa, what should be done with the workshop gauge?
o: Fail it, tag it out of use and send it for adjustment
Pass it, since its readings at 0 and 1,000 kPa are close
Pass it, but take 22 kPa off every reading from now on
Fail it, but keep using it until the next calibration date
questions.why: At 750 kPa the errors (+20 rising and +22 falling) are outside ±16 kPa, so the gauge fails. A failed gauge is tagged out of use and sent for adjustment or replacement. Correcting readings by hand is unreliable, because the error is different at each point.

questions.q: Why does Mr Edwards insist on taking readings with the pressure falling as well as rising?
o: Falling readings let the reference gauge cool down
A gauge may read differently going down than going up
It doubles the number of readings, so the average is better
Gauges are only tested on falling pressure in a plant
questions.why: Friction and springiness in the movement can make a gauge read differently on rising and falling pressure. This is hysteresis. Here the falling readings were higher than the rising ones at most points, and the worst error appeared on the way down.

questions.q: For the thermometer check, why does Mr Edwards pack the cup with crushed ice and add only enough water to fill the gaps, then stir?
o: So the thermometer reads faster than in warm water
So that the ice does not melt during the whole test
So the mixture all round the stem is at 0 °C
So that the thermometer reads 32 °F instead of 0 °C
questions.why: A well-stirred mixture of crushed ice and a little water settles at 0 °C. Too much water, or lumps of ice, leave pockets of warmer water round the stem and give a false error. Wait until the reading is steady before recording it.

questions.q: Nicola measures 14 mA in the transmitter loop. How deep is the water?
questions.why: Depth = (current − 4) ÷ 16 × range = (14 − 4) ÷ 16 × 4 = 10 ÷ 16 × 4 = 2.5 m. Dividing 14 by 4 (3.5 m) forgets that the signal starts at 4 mA, not 0.

questions.q: One morning the office display shows 0 mA, but the sight glass shows plenty of water. What is the most likely cause?
o: The loop is broken or the transmitter has lost power
The tank is empty, so the pumps must be stopped at once
The tank is overflowing, so the transmitter has cut out
The water is at 0 m, which is normal early in the morning
questions.why: An empty tank would still give 4 mA. A reading of 0 mA, below the live zero, means the signal itself has failed: a broken wire, a lost supply or a failed transmitter. Report it, and use the sight glass for the level until it is repaired.

questions.q: The pressure gauge at the bottom of the tank reads 25 kPa. Does this agree with a water depth of 2.5 m?
o: No: 25 kPa means there is 25 m of water above it
No: the gauge must be read in bar before comparing
Yes: each metre of water adds about 10 kPa
Yes: for water, kPa and metres are the same unit
questions.why: Each metre of water adds about 9.8 kPa, roughly 10 kPa, so 25 kPa is about 2.5 m of water above the gauge. Two different methods that agree give you confidence in the reading.

questions.q: A flow meter reads 3 m³/h, but the log sheet asks for litres per minute. What should be written?
o: 180 L/min
50 L/min
3,000 L/min
0.05 L/min
questions.why: 3 m³ = 3,000 L, so 3 m³/h = 3,000 L per hour. An hour has 60 minutes: 3,000 ÷ 60 = 50 L/min.

questions.q: A 0–600 kPa gauge is accuracy class 1.6 (±1.6% of full scale). How far out may its reading be at any point on the scale?
o: ±1.6 kPa
±16 kPa
±9.6 kPa
questions.why: 1.6% of full scale is 0.016 × 600 = 9.6 kPa, so a reading may be up to 9.6 kPa high or low anywhere on the scale. Near the bottom of the scale this is a large share of the reading, which is one reason to keep normal readings near mid-scale.

questions.q: On four weekly rounds, a pump bearing's vibration reads 2.1, 2.4, 3.6 and 5.8 mm/s. The plant's alarm level is 7.1 mm/s. What should be done?
o: Nothing yet, since every reading is below the alarm level
Report the rising trend so the bearing is checked soon
Re-zero the vibration meter, as it must be drifting
Write 2.1 mm/s each week until the bearing is replaced
questions.why: Each reading is inside the limit, but the trend is climbing faster every week, a typical warning of a failing bearing or misalignment. Reporting it now lets the pump be checked before it fails. Never record a figure you did not measure.
